Hello Eric
Thanks for your thoughts, really helpful.
Only one individual was repeated across the two surveys (2012 and 2016), giving us a confidence to consider each session as independent.

So, please correct me if I am wrong. You suggest running a multi-session analyses with the below list of models:

g0~1
g0~h2
g0~bk
g0~b
g0~Bk
g0~t
g0~session
sigma~session

For 2016, we had only one male, so sex is not a proper covariate to be considered.

My two major concerns are still there:

First, how to report higher density when fewer leopard detected, to decision makers?

Second, the g0 of 0.005 still looks very low, in similar studies on leopards in Iran we got g0 of around 15-20%.

Any thought is highly appreciated.

Best wishes, Mohammad

On Friday, September 27, 2019 at 4:53:28 PM UTC+1, Eric H wrote:
> Dear Mohammad,
>
> Just a few thoughts:
>
> Estimates of g0 are specific to a single trap, as well as to occasions and individuals. It's the probability of detecting an animal at a trap located at it's activity center, on one occasion.  You have many occasions, so estimates may not be unreasonably low.
>
> As you suggest, the large difference in movements likely explains why you obtained a higher density estimate in 2012 (buffer size could possibly be an issue - it should be large enough to accommodate longer movements [e.g. 3 or 4 times sigma from winter]).
>
> If home range size or movement rate differs between seasons, it could be difficult to separate differences across years from seasonal effects, especially if none of the same animals were detected in both 2012 and 2016.
>
> Modelling the difference in sigma between sessions in a multisession analysis might help.  However, the difference in movements is large so it would likely be supported by model selection criteria.  You will get similar density estimates in the two years from a multisession analysis with session effects on g0 and sigma as when the data were modelled separately. "Sessions" are usually assumed to be independent (different animals, non-overlapping data).
>
> However, if some of the same animals were detected in 2012 and 2016 (and can be recognized across years) open population SCR models might allow you to model seasonal differences in sigma, and possibly to estimate survival and to detect a change in density across years.  The abundance of recaptures in your data should help inform probabilities of mortality vs failure to detect an animal that was present.
>
> Good luck,
> Eric
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mohammad,

Regarding the model set, I'd suggest retaining any effects you're already considering, and replicating the model set, adding session effects to g0, sigma, and both parameters, in 3 replicates. Not sure how many effects the data will support, and I expect session effects (at least on sigma) will be supported, so you would likely get similar results.

Regarding reporting the results, you could explain that the higher estimate from fewer animals is a consequence of the movement rate (more animals were present but were using smaller areas, so fewer were detected). Or, concede that the differences between seasons make it hard to draw inferences about relative density.

Carefully consider Murray's comments about array size and shape with respect to home range size and shape. See Marques et al. 2011: A hierarchical model for spatial capture–recapture data: commenty, and Efford 2011. Estimation of population density by spatially explicit capture–recapture analysis of data from area searches, and Efford 2019. Non‐circular home ranges and the estimation of population density. All were published in Ecology.

Eric

messages.subject: minnrRSE / relative standard error
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am looking into using the secrdesign package as a way of validating some subset scenarios I have run for my species. I am interested in the relative standard error (RSE) of estimated density that is discussed a lot in the new Efford and Boulanger (2019) paper "fast evaluation of study designs for spatially explicit capture-recapture". I am not running simulations, but subsetting my own empirical data as we have a wealth of data and several populations.

The paper states that "For many scenarios the relative standard error (RSE) of estimated density is close to 1∕√min{E(n),E(r)". I have been looking through the secrdesign vignettes and the appendices from this paper to determine how to calculate RSE for my data. I have been using the function minnrRSE, but am not clear if I am using it correctly for determining RSE for each of my scenarios - or if there is a simple equation I should be using instead.

This is an example of the code:

library(secrdesign)
subset <- minnrRSE(densityestimate, traps = trapsfile, mask = maskfile, detectpar = list(lambda0 = lambdaestimate, sigma = sigmaestimate), noccasions = 3, detectfn = "HEX")

For densityestimate, lambdaestimate and sigmaestimate, I have been using the density, lambda, and sigma estimates from my empirical model. We had three occasions and all models were run with the HEX detection function. Is this the correct method for calculating RSE of an empirical run?

Thank you,
Samantha

messages.subject: Re: minnrRSE / relative standard error
messages.body_plain:
The relative standard error of an estimate is the estimated standard error of the estimate divided by the estimate, as on the second page of the paper. For parameters on the log scale this may also be got directly from the variance of the logs. Hence
pred <- predict(secrdemo.0)
pred['D','SE.estimate'] / pred['D','estimate']
# [1] 0.1180226
sqrt(exp(vcov(secrdemo.0)['D','D']) - 1)
# [1] 0.1180226

I am suspicious of sub-sampling approaches - there is a risk that if you condition on a particular dataset you may miss relevant variance.

messages.body_plain:
Hi
moving.fit is an experimental solution to the problem of too much data, so I'm not going to die in a ditch for it, but...
i. get this working with a simple, fast, possibly non-spatial, model before laboring over a spatial full ~t model (though JSSAsecrfCL is a good starting point for open spatial analyses)
ii. incorporate all the sampling intervals in your data - doesn't make sense to provide them like this, especially as you provide 4 when there are two intervals in width-3 subset of sessions.
iii. analysing only 3 sessions at a time is very likely to expose weaknesses - open population methods work best with long series; end estimates are the most biased, and with width=3 all estimates are end estimates.
iv. have you tried every other avenue to speed it up (e.g. mask of only about 1000 points; collapsing secondary sessions)?
Murray

This is a problem specific to AICc with very small sample sizes (when the number of parameters is greater than or equal to the number of individuals). Murray

messages.body_plain:
Good day,

I'm still working up comparisons of varD from replicate sampling units under different assumptions (detection parameters assumed to be constant or variable across replicates, Poisson vs empirical variances).

Two questions about these variance estimators, and their application in 'secr':

(1)  I'm looking at Buckland et al. (2001), Fewster et al. (2009), and, Murray's "replicateclusters.pdf" from 17-12-2018 in this thread.

In "replicateclusters" the first equation for the encounter rate variance for unequal line lengths in DS surveys matches Buckland et al.'s (2001) Equation 3.78 (page 79) for var(n), and the first equation for var(n) from an SECR survey with replicate sampling units is an exact match (substituting a's and A's for l's and L's, respectively).

However, varR2(n) from an SECR survey in replicateclusters.pdf is not an exact match for Fewster et al's (2009) varR2(n/L) from DS surveys (their Equation 3).  In Fewster et al, (k-1) is multiplied by L-squared (total line length squared) in the denominator of the first term, but there is no corresponding multiplication by A-squared (total effective sampling area squared).  Hoping someone can confirm for me that this is the adjustment to estimate var(n) rather than var(n/A) as described in "replicateclusters.pdf"? Thanks very much.

(2) My second question has to do with when replicates should be considered independent, and the 'independent.esa' argument of the derivednj function.
Our replicates each have ~40 traps, and yielded sufficient data to estimate density in isolation; animals are not detected at > 1 replicate.  I can fit models to "replicate-specific" data, harvest n, a-sub-j, and the SE of a-sub-j from each (using derived), and calculate D and associated measures of uncertainty using derivednj. In this situation, sets of animals are independent, and no information is shared across replicates when estimating detection parameters, so I set indepdendent.esa = T.

I'm also fitting models to multisession data with replicates as sessions (to facilitate comparisons). In this situation, sets of animals do not overlap, but information is shared when estimating the parameters of the detection function, even if I include (additive) session effects. In this situation, since data is shared, should I set independent.esa = F? Thanks again.

Eric

                  start = start.mod, trace = T, ncores = 4, buffer = 2000)
four <- secr.fit(input.data, mask = NULL, model = list(D ~ 1, g0 ~ t + session + hog, sigma ~ session + t),

Hi James
Without delving too deeply into your example - I suspect your models fitted just fine and the problem comes in 'predicting' real parameter estimates. For example, AIC(three, four) should be OK?

For time-varying trap covariates you must use the 'newdata' argument of predict() to specify the levels for which you want estimates. Thus predict(three, newdata=data.frame(hog = ...). This is shown in the Examples of the ?timevarying help. Not sure where it is documented otherwise. (I'm sceptical in general about fully time-specific (t) models, and there may be difficulty if trap covariates are also time-varying).
Murray

I am a MSc student brand new to secr (and still working on learning R) and I have a question about setting up my trap and capture history tables. I am working on small mammals (primarily mice) and I used Sherman traps. I have everything pretty much set, but I don't know how to include information about the mice that happened to escape my technicians during handling before an eartag was placed. I've been researching this problem and I can't seem to find an example of a solution. I don't think I can just omit this data from the dataset, because the traps were closed and thus unavailable for another mouse to be caught, which seems to me like it would impact the trap effort. I had thought about just setting the trap effort for the traps these escapees were caught in as 0.5 (which I am doing for traps that closed without catching anything), but I wasn't sure if this was the appropriate solution or not. Any help would be appreciated and I apologize for the basic question.

Cheers,

Jen
